subtopic: Planning a legacy or purpose project
subtype: Approach: grand vision with no first step [Pitfall]
passage: For eight months Kiran told anyone who'd listen about the plan to transform education across the state. There was a forty-slide deck, three logo options, and a name argued over with Manoj, a friend, on long tea breaks. Kiran also had a full-time job and only Sunday mornings free. Whenever Manoj asked, 'What can we do this month?' Kiran said the idea was too big for small steps. Teaching one class felt silly next to a whole state. One Sunday a heavy monsoon kept the two indoors, and Manoj asked to see the calendar: not one meeting with a school, not one test of an idea. The deck was polished, and nothing else existed. Kiran closed the laptop and said nothing for a while.

qa.q: How many logo options did Kiran have?
Why did Kiran resist small steps?
qa.a: Kiran felt the dream was so large that teaching one class seemed silly next to a whole state, so any first step felt too small.

qa.q: What other approach could Kiran use to get started?
qa.a: Kiran could pick one school and run a small pilot on a Sunday morning, since a real class would teach more than another version of the deck.

qa.q: How might Manoj see the deck and the months of talk?
qa.a: Manoj probably sees a lot of effort with nothing tested and feels frustrated, and asking to see the calendar shows worry for Kiran.

grounding: Shows a person with a huge dream to change education, months of presentations and logos, and no first action, because the size makes small steps seem pointless.
